paragraphs.heading: A library that became an academy
paragraphs.text: The House of Wisdom, Bayt al-Hikmah in Arabic, was a major academy and centre of learning in Baghdad in the time of the Abbasid caliphs. Its start is uncertain. It may have begun in the late 8th century as a library for the books of the caliph Harun al-Rashid, or as a private collection of the earlier caliph al-Mansur, kept to hold rare books in Arabic. Under the caliph al-Ma'mun, who ruled from 813 to 833, it became a public academy and library. It was destroyed in 1258, when the Mongols besieged Baghdad.

paragraphs.heading: Roots in Damascus
paragraphs.text: A royal collection of books had been tried before. Under the earlier Umayyad dynasty, Muawiyah I gathered books in Damascus into a library that was also called Bayt al-Hikma. Muslim scholars of that time collected and translated books in Greek, Latin and Persian on medicine, alchemy, physics, mathematics and astrology. The Umayyads also took paper-making methods from the Chinese and hired Christian and Persian scholars both to translate and to create new knowledge. In 750 the Abbasids replaced the Umayyads, and in 762 the caliph al-Mansur built Baghdad and made it his capital in place of Damascus.

paragraphs.heading: The Translation Movement
paragraphs.text: The Abbasids borrowed many customs from the Sasanian Empire, including the translation of foreign books, though now the books were put into Arabic. Al-Mansur set up a palace library modelled on the Sasanian imperial library and backed the scholars there with money and political support. He also invited groups of scholars from India and elsewhere to share their mathematics and astronomy. Books in Greek, Chinese, Sanskrit, Persian and Syriac were all turned into Arabic. This Translation Movement sped up under Harun al-Rashid; it began mainly with medicine, mathematics and astronomy, and philosophy soon followed.

paragraphs.heading: One centre among several
paragraphs.text: The House of Wisdom was part of this movement, but it was probably not its only home, since major translation work began in Cairo and Damascus even earlier. With Greek, Persian and Indian texts in hand, scholars in the Muslim world went on to original research. New work in mathematics, astronomy, philosophy and medicine marked the start of Arabic science, and that in turn created demand for more and newer translations. Baghdad drew Arab, Persian and other scholars because it was the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate.

paragraphs.heading: Scholars at work
paragraphs.text: Inside, writers, translators, scientists, scribes and others met every day to translate, write, read and talk. The scholars also served the city outside the library. They often worked as engineers and architects on large building projects, kept the official calendars, and acted as public servants, doctors and advisers. Al-Ma'mun took a close personal interest, visiting the scholars often, asking about their work, and even joining and judging their debates.

paragraphs.heading: Books as prizes of war
paragraphs.text: Abbasid society itself came to value learning, and merchants and the army gave support too. Scholars and translators could earn a living easily, and an academic life signalled high standing. Knowledge was prized so much that books and ancient texts were sometimes taken as war booty in place of riches. After the Abbasids fought a war with the Eastern Roman Empire, al-Ma'mun is said to have demanded Ptolemy's Almagest as a condition for peace.
